what_its_for: Mifepristone is used for two main purposes. First, it is used to end an early pregnancy (up to 10 weeks) when used together with another medicine called misoprostol. Second, a higher-dose version (Korlym) is used to control high blood sugar in adults with a certain condition called Cushing's syndrome who also have type 2 diabetes or pre-diabetes.
how_to_take: Take mifepristone exactly as your doctor or healthcare provider tells you. Swallow the tablet whole with a full glass of water. You can take it with or without food. If you are using it to end a pregnancy, you will take mifepristone first, and then take a second medicine called misoprostol 24 to 48 hours later as directed by your doctor. Do not take more than prescribed, and follow all instructions given to you by your healthcare provider or clinic very carefully.
dosing: For ending a pregnancy (Mifeprex): The usual dose is one 200 mg tablet taken by mouth at your doctor's office or clinic. For Cushing's syndrome (Korlym): The starting dose is usually 300 mg once daily by mouth, and your doctor may slowly increase your dose over time up to a maximum of 1200 mg per day. Your specific dose depends on your medical condition, other medicines you take, and how your body responds to treatment. Always follow your doctor's exact instructions.
missed_dose: If you are using Korlym for Cushing's syndrome and you miss a dose, take it as soon as you remember that same day. If it is almost time for your next scheduled dose, skip the missed dose and continue with your regular schedule. Do not take two doses at the same time to make up for a missed one. If you are using Mifeprex to end a pregnancy, it is very important to follow the schedule your doctor gave you exactly. Call your doctor or clinic right away if you miss or delay any part of the treatment.
storage: Store mifepristone tablets at room temperature, between 68°F and 77°F (20°C and 25°C). Keep the medicine in its original packaging. Keep it away from heat, direct sunlight, and moisture. Do not store it in the bathroom. Keep all medicines out of reach of children and pets. Dispose of any unused medicine safely — ask your pharmacist how to properly throw away medicines you no longer need.
what_to_avoid: Avoid taking ibuprofen (Advil, Motrin) or other non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs (NSAIDs) during your treatment, as they may interfere with how the medicine works. Avoid grapefruit and grapefruit juice, as it can increase the amount of medicine in your blood and raise the risk of side effects. Do not take St. John's Wort, as it can make the medicine less effective. Tell your doctor about all prescription, over-the-counter, and herbal medicines you take, because many medicines can interact with mifepristone. Avoid alcohol during treatment. Do not breastfeed while taking mifepristone.
when_to_call_doctor: Call your doctor or go to the emergency room right away if you have any of the following: very heavy bleeding (soaking more than 2 thick pads per hour for 2 hours in a row), severe stomach or belly pain that does not get better with pain medicine, fever of 100.4°F (38°C) or higher that lasts more than 24 hours, foul-smelling vaginal discharge, dizziness, fainting, or feel very weak. Also call your doctor if you have signs of an allergic reaction such as hives, rash, swelling of the face or throat, or trouble breathing. For Korlym users, call your doctor if you have unusual tiredness, muscle weakness, irregular heartbeat, or swelling in your hands or feet.
when_it_works: If you are using mifepristone to end a pregnancy, the process takes a few days and requires two medicines. Mifepristone starts working by blocking the hormones needed for the pregnancy to continue. After you take the second medicine (misoprostol) 24 to 48 hours later, cramping and bleeding usually begin within 1 to 4 hours. A follow-up visit with your doctor about 7 to 14 days later is very important to make sure the treatment worked completely. For Cushing's syndrome (Korlym), it may take several weeks before you notice improvement in your blood sugar levels. Your doctor will monitor your progress with regular check-ups.
special_populations: Pregnancy: Mifepristone used as Mifeprex is specifically intended to end a pregnancy and should not be used by people who wish to continue their pregnancy. Korlym is NOT safe during pregnancy and can cause serious harm to an unborn baby. If you are taking Korlym and can become pregnant, you must use a reliable non-hormonal birth control method during treatment and for one month after stopping. Breastfeeding: Do not breastfeed while taking mifepristone. Children: Mifepristone is not approved for use in children. Older adults and people with liver or kidney disease: Use with extra caution. Your doctor may need to adjust your dose or monitor you more closely. Always tell your doctor your full medical history before starting this medicine.
